primary_sources: Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899

stimulus.source_note: Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899, public domain.
stimulus.text: "Take up the White Man's burden — Send forth the best ye breed — Go bind your sons to exile To serve your captives' need; To wait in heavy harness, On fluttered folk and wild — Your new-caught, sullen peoples, Half-devil and half-child. Take up the White Man's burden — In patience to abide, To veil the threat of terror And check the show of pride; By open speech and simple, An hundred times made plain To seek another's profit, And work another's gain." — Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt (first two stanzas) from Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899, public domain.
stem: Kipling's poem urges its readers to accept which of the following?

options.text: Ruling the peoples he calls "half-devil and half-child"
The independence of the Philippines from American rule
options.misconception: Kipling urges the opposite: he tells Americans to take up ruling the Philippines, not to set them free.

options.text: A return to governing only the North American continent
options.misconception: The poem sends readers outward, to exile among new peoples. Staying home is the opposite of its call.

options.text: An end to trade with China
options.misconception: The poem says nothing about China trade. Its subject is the duty of ruling other peoples.

rationales.A: The poem's call is a duty: take up the burden and rule the "new-caught, sullen peoples," described as half-devil and half-child.
rationales.B: Kipling urges the opposite of independence. He tells Americans to take up ruling the Philippines, not to set them free.
rationales.C: The poem sends readers outward, to exile among new peoples. Staying home is the opposite of its call.
rationales.D: The poem says nothing about China trade. Its subject is the duty of ruling other peoples.
rationales.general:
1. Find the repeated command. "Take up the White Man's burden" opens both stanzas, so it is the poem's point.
2. Ask what the burden is. It is ruling the "new-caught, sullen peoples" Kipling calls half-devil and half-child.
3. Check the other options. Independence, staying home, and ending China trade all run against the command.
4. Put it together. Kipling frames empire as a duty to accept, not a prize to enjoy.
Remember: a poem's repeated line is usually its argument in short.
